paragraphs.source_en: 'This gentleman called Miss Onatsu and asked, 'Are there watermelons in Shizuoka?' Miss Onatsu replied, 'Shizuoka may be a small place, but of course we have watermelons.' Then she brought in a tray piled high with sliced watermelon, and Rōbai, they say, began eating it. He polished off the whole heap of watermelon and then waited for Miss Onatsu's answer. Before the answer came, the gentleman's stomach began to ache. He groaned and bore it, but it would not improve, so he called Miss Onatsu again and asked whether there was a doctor in Shizuoka. Miss Onatsu said that Shizuoka might be small, but of course it had doctors. Then she brought a doctor with a name that sounded stolen from the Thousand Character Classic, something like 'Heaven Earth Dark Yellow.' By early the next morning his stomachache had been cured, and naturally the gentleman was delighted. Fifteen minutes before leaving the inn, he summoned Miss Onatsu and asked whether she accepted his proposal of marriage from the day before. Miss Onatsu answered with a smile, 'Shizuoka has watermelons, and it has doctors, but it has no brides who agree in a single night.' With that she went away and never showed her face again. After that, Rōbai, like me, became a disappointed lover. And as for the library, they say he never went there again except to relieve himself. When you think it over, women are sinful creatures indeed.'

paragraphs.source_en: Hearing this lofty discourse from her husband, the master's wife naturally refused to let it pass. She said, 'You may say frivolous women are no good, but heavy men are not necessarily any better.' The master said, 'Heavy? What do you mean by that?' 'Heavy means heavy, of course. Like you!' 'How am I heavy?' 'Are you not heavy?' The husband and wife began arguing, though over what exactly no one could tell. Meitei listened with great amusement for a while, then opened his mouth and said, 'For you two to grow red in the face and attack each other with arguments like this is precisely what one might call the true form of marriage. Married couples in the old style must surely have been utterly meaningless.' He spoke so ambiguously that it was impossible to tell whether he was praising them or mocking them. paragraphs.source_en: 'They say that in the old days not a single woman dared answer her husband back, but if that is so it is no different from marrying a mute, and I for one cannot approve. I would much rather be told something like, 'Are you not heavy?' as you do, madam. If one is going to take a wife, unless one quarrels once or twice now and then, surely one would be bored to death. Take my mother: whenever she came before my father, all she ever said was 'yes' or 'hmm.' And in twenty years of marriage, aside from going to the temple to visit the ancestral graves, they never once went out together. Is that not pitiful? Still, I suppose it had its advantages: my mother knew every posthumous Buddhist name on the ancestral gravestones by heart. Relations between men and women were not permitted either; when I was a child, it would have been utterly impossible to do as Kangetsu does, playing music with the beloved, exchanging spirits, meeting in a hazy trance, and so forth.'
